leading_positions.synthesis: All eight round-1 files state the same preferred configuration: a single prize part for B013, optical lattice clocks, to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The citations differ only in wording (10^-18 level timekeeping, a new regime of precision in measuring time, magic-wavelength trapping). Several members moved to B013 from other opening first choices (Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig, Pearce), so the convergence comes from reading the other ballots as well as from opening preferences. What is shared is the merit case (magic-wavelength removal of light-shift and motional errors, near 1e-18 uncertainty, comparisons across independent laboratories, uses in redshift tests, constants, dark matter and the SI second) and the view that a two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist. What is not shared is how much weight the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes and the omitted lattice-clock groups should carry. No file proposes a second prize part. The alternatives named behind B013 are scattered: B046 (Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig), B001 (Johansson, Olsson, Pearce), B015 (Eriksson, Olsson), B037 (Kroll, Lindroth), B059 (Pearce), B016 (Danielsson), B054 (Johansson), B009 (Kroll), B050 (Lindroth), B042 (Mehlig).

areas_of_agreement: All eight members explicitly prefer B013 for Katori and Ye as the sole prize part in their round-1 configuration.

Members describe the scientific case in the same terms: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light-shift and motional problem, and strontium lattice clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18.
Members point to independent reproduction and mutual comparison across several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) as evidence of maturity.
Members cite concrete consequences: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the road map to redefining the second.

All eight members describe the Katori and Ye pairing as the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, avoiding the large-collaboration naming problems of other candidates; Olsson adds that a two-person prize leaves no arbitrary exclusions inside a collaboration. Every member also lists, as a reservation, that other groups are not credited.

Seven members (all but Pearce) name the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 prizes as the main objection or a point the committee must test; Pearce raises Ye's 2005 prize and the same-laboratory-family concern. No member treats the overlap as disqualifying.
scientific_disputes: Eriksson, Kroll, Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Danielsson raise whether lattice clocks add a distinct achievement beyond the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes or are an incremental step on a line already honoured; Mehlig lists 1989, 1997, 2001, 2005 and 2012 as earlier recognition in precision metrology.

Eriksson, Danielsson and Mehlig state that their taste runs toward a new state of matter, a new window on nature or deeper conceptual reach (B046, B016, B042). Eriksson and Danielsson describe clocks as a technique or as useful rather than existential; Mehlig says B042 has deeper conceptual reach but almost no support in this committee.

Johansson asks whether superconducting circuits are already covered by the 2025 prize, which bears on B054 and, through the same question, on how far a further quantum-circuit award rests on distinct physics. Pearce raised the same point.

Pearce notes that broad support may reflect clear attribution as much as scientific weight and that the Higgs discovery (B001) arguably has greater weight with a structurally hard attribution problem; Johansson and Olsson keep B001 as an alternative.
attribution_disputes: Every member records that Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko, Oates, Bloom and the SYRTE, PTB, NIST and Yb or Sr groups made real contributions that a two-name credit omits; Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Eriksson ask whether the citation should mention them or be phrased around invention and realisation to limit the problem. Several members say they have not verified early priority dates.

Olsson asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for the same achievement or for two separable contributions, Katori's invention and first strontium lattice clock versus Ye's record accuracy and many-body clock, and says the prize should reward the original work rather than a second group that did it much better.

Ye already shared the 2005 prize (Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce); members differ on how much that matters for a 2026 pairing, and Pearce makes it his stated reason for B001 or B059 as fallback.

Alternatives raise separate credit problems: B001 requires choosing among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee from two collaborations; B016 (Falcke, Doeleman, Zensus, with Pearce arguing Zensus cannot be omitted); B046 (the credited trio omits Yuan Cao and others); B015 (Krivanek and Dellby priority on the STEM corrector); B009 (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth); B050 (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller); B042 (Parisi already a laureate, and Takeuchi's experiments plus exact solutions come from further people); B059 (Halzen, Karle, Spiering against AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal pioneers).
maturity_disputes: Kroll and Olsson note that the redefinition of the second has not happened, and that its largest payoff may be still to come; Kroll asks whether to wait for it, Olsson whether a different year would suit better. Danielsson and Mehlig treat the more than twenty years of reproduction as ample maturity.

Pearce, Mehlig, Lindroth, Johansson and Olsson (as reported by Pearce) point to the unresolved superconducting mechanism and the short time since the 2018 experiments as reasons B046 may be premature; Eriksson asks whether B046 should wait for the pairing mechanism, while still ranking it first at opening.
Pearce asks whether IceCube source identification beyond the diffuse flux has matured enough for B059, a concern Danielsson accepts.
Danielsson (as stated by Pearce) would want more polarization and dynamics results before backing B016.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson: B054 (circuit QED) lies in his own field, he directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, works with Chalmers superconducting-circuit groups and knows the credited people; he states he should be recused from advocating or voting on B054 and treats his first-place ranking of it as potentially biased. He reports no connection to B013.

Olsson: B015 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in her own field, electron microscopy; she would consider recusing herself from any decision on B015. She also shares Chalmers with Johansson. She reports no conflict for B013.

Lindroth: long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and close to atomic structure and many-body theory, so professionally close to B013 and B050; she reports no connection with Katori or Ye and no conflict requiring recusal.

Kroll: alternatives B009 and B037 sit near his quantum optics and sensing interests, and his Wallenberg Centre role overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home at Chalmers (relevant to B054, not B013); no conflict for B013.

Pearce (chair): member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, working in astroparticle physics adjacent to B059 and B016; he states no personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals and no recusal-level conflict for B013 or B001.

Eriksson: computational work connected to electron spectroscopy and 2D materials, with no tie to credited individuals; Mehlig: same Gothenburg physics environment as Chalmers colleagues, with no collaboration with them or any credited candidate; Danielsson: no conflict, though his first-ranked B016 is near his interest in black holes. None reports a conflict for B013.
questions_for_round2: Does B013 stand as a distinct achievement given the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and what specific new science or capability beyond those prizes should the citation name?

Is Katori and Ye the right credit, or should the committee name Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Takamoto or other groups? Which members can verify early strontium and ytterbium lattice-clock priority dates and the relative roles of Katori and Ye?

Should the citation separate Katori's magic-wavelength invention and first lattice clock from Ye's record accuracy and stability, and would that wording meet Olsson's concern about rewarding the original work?
Does the pending redefinition of the second argue for awarding B013 now or for waiting, and does any member's support depend on the answer?

Is any member's support for B013 conditional on a second prize part, given that no file proposes one? If a second part is wanted, which candidate (B001, B046, B059, B015, B016, B054, B037) has a defensible attribution within the three-person limit alongside the two names for B013?
If a member whose own first or alternative candidate is B054 or B015 is to recuse, how should the committee treat Johansson's and Olsson's statements on those candidates in round 2?

Can the B001 attribution among ATLAS and CMS leaders be settled by committee consensus, or is it excluded for that reason alone? How does the committee weigh scientific weight against attribution clarity here?
summary.chair_observation: The round-1 files are unusually aligned: all eight, including the chair, name B013 alone for Katori and Ye, and five moved to it after reading the other ballots. Alignment on a configuration does not settle the dispute over precedent, since every file lists the same reservations about the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the omitted lattice-clock groups. Round 2 should test those reservations, not only count agreement, and should give the minority interests (B046, B001, B016, B015, B054, B042, B037) a fair hearing.
